---
title: "Metric Dependence in Seasonal Heat-Stress Timing"
description: "Heat metrics can move together hour-to-hour yet identify different periods as the hottest part of the year."
status: "Manuscript in preparation"
year: 2026
---

## Research question

When heat-action planning targets the hottest part of the year, do commonly used heat-stress metrics agree on **when** that period occurs?

## Approach

Using hourly ERA5 reanalysis for India from 1980–2024, we compute, for every grid cell and year, the contiguous 90-day period maximizing four metrics: 2 m air temperature, Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), and Extended Heat Index (EHI), and compare their start dates.

## Headline results

- The metrics track one another closely hour-to-hour, with Spearman correlations of about **0.84–0.97**.
- They nevertheless peak in sequence: **temperature → UTCI → EHI → WBGT**.
- Over the Indo-Gangetic Plain, WBGT- and temperature-defined 90-day windows differ by about **seven weeks in the median**.
- At roughly a fifth of grid cells, those windows fail to overlap at all in at least one year.
- Among the hottest decile of hours—the observations that determine the seasonal maximum—temperature and WBGT lose essentially all rank association in 2024 (**Kendall's τ = −0.06**).
- The share of years in which a metric selects the humid season rises through the metric sequence, reaching **0.47 for WBGT**.

## High correlation does not guarantee agreement in extremes

The central result is a scale paradox: the metrics can look highly interchangeable over the full hourly distribution while disagreeing strongly in the upper tail that actually determines the hottest sustained period.

### 1. The metrics are highly correlated at representative grid points

<figure class="research-figure research-figure-wide">
<a href="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-hourly-correlation.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-hourly-correlation.png" alt="Six representative pair plots showing strong Spearman correlations among air temperature, EHI, UTCI and WBGT."></a>
<figcaption><strong>Strong hourly correlation coexists with divergent extremes.</strong> For each metric pair, the panel uses the 2024 hourly values at the grid cell holding the median long-run start-date difference for that pair. The upper triangles show rank correlations, the diagonals show each metric's distribution, and the lower triangles show scatter with LOWESS fits. The central clouds are tight and near-linear, while the hot tails curve and fan. These raw-hourly correlations include the seasonal and diurnal cycles shared by the metrics, so they should not be read as evidence that the metrics are interchangeable in the extreme tail.</figcaption>
</figure>

### 2. The hottest tail is much more discordant

<figure class="research-figure research-figure-narrow">
<a href="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-top-decile-discordance.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-top-decile-discordance.png" alt="Maps of pairwise discordant-pair fractions for full-hourly data and for top-decile hours anchored on UTCI or WBGT."></a>
<figcaption><strong>Discordance rises sharply in the hottest tail.</strong> The left column shows the discordant-pair fraction over the full hourly record; the middle and right columns restrict attention to the hottest 10% of hours, anchored on UTCI and WBGT respectively. Pairwise ordering is far more stable across the full distribution than among the observations that decide the seasonal extreme. In the 2024 archive, temperature and WBGT lose essentially all rank association in this hottest decile (Kendall's τ = −0.06).</figcaption>
</figure>

### 3. Tail disagreement is enough to move the 90-day maximum by weeks

<figure class="research-figure research-figure-narrow">
<a href="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-blockmax-timing.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-blockmax-timing.png" alt="Maps of pairwise differences in the timing of maximizing 90-day heat-stress windows across India, including 2024 differences, long-run medians and Sen-slope trends."></a>
<figcaption><strong>Pairwise disagreement in the timing of the hottest quarter is large and signed.</strong> Rows show the six metric pairs (U = UTCI, W = WBGT, T = air temperature, H = Extended Heat Index), with differences taken in the order the letters appear, so red/positive means the first metric peaks later. Columns show the 2024 difference in 90-day block-maximum end date, the long-run median difference, and the Sen's-slope trend over 1980–2024. The first two columns saturate at ±40 days, so still-larger differences—including non-overlapping windows with |Δ| > 90 days—appear at the colour-scale limits. This is the key consequence: modest-looking differences in the ordering of the hottest hours are sufficient to move the selected 90-day maximum by many weeks.</figcaption>
</figure>

Together, the three figures show why an overall correlation coefficient is not sufficient for deciding whether heat-stress metrics are interchangeable for seasonal planning. **The relevant question is whether they preserve ordering in the extreme part of the distribution that selects the maximum window.**

## Metric choice as a normative choice

Different heat metrics encode different physical and physiological emphases: temperature, humidity, radiation, wind, or combinations of them. A warning calendar therefore does not simply *measure* a pre-existing hottest season; it operationalises a definition of heat stress and thereby determines whose exposures receive policy attention.

This is one example of the modelling approach I want to develop more broadly: identify where technical definitions carry normative consequences, then quantify how much those choices change the conclusion.

Figures, code, and manuscript links will continue to be added as the paper is finalized.
